release.title: The Studio: the final weeks
release.html:
Pavilion of the Republic of Armenia at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia

Zadik Zadikian: The Studio. The final weeks

Venice, 31 October 2026

Zadik Zadikian: The Studio, the National Participation of the Republic of Armenia, closes on Sunday 22 November 2026. Until then the Armenian Pavilion stays what it has been since May: a working sculpture studio in Tesa 41, Arsenale Militare, open Tuesday to Sunday.

In 1974 Richard Serra titled one of his first installation drawings Zadikians, after the young artist then working in his studio. The drawing is in the collection of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum. It was in Serra's studio, in 1973, that Zadik Zadikian met Tony Shafrazi, now the Pavilion's curator.

Zadikian went on to open both of Shafrazi's galleries. On 31 October 1978, Gold Bricks opened at Tony Shafrazi Gallery in Tehran. It was about a thousand gilded bricks, and it was the gallery's first and only exhibition. After the Revolution the bricks were stolen from storage. A year later, from 16 October to 5 November 1979, Zadik Zadikian: Sculptures opened Tony Shafrazi Gallery in New York.

In Venice he has spent six months making his work in public. With his son Aram Zadikian, who runs the studio, and seven students of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia as his assistants, Zadikian casts plaster units with the pigment mixed through the material. The units are stacked, taken apart and stacked again, and they stay separate and movable. Hundreds have been cast since the opening. A visitor sees the work at whatever stage it has reached that day: plaster poured, pigment mixed, surfaces sanded, a stack rebuilt.

"I leave spaces between my blocks, my units, so that they can breathe," Zadikian says.

The Venice project follows Path to Nine (2024), 999 gilded plaster ingots in eighteen stacks, shown in Solid Gold at the Brooklyn Museum (16 November 2024 – 6 July 2025).

In Minor Keys, the 61st International Art Exhibition, was conceived by Koyo Kouoh around listening, slowness and work made in common. The curators of the Armenian Pavilion, Tony Shafrazi and Tina Chakarian, treat the studio itself as the exhibit. The making is on view on every open day, and the room has changed week by week since May. Shafrazi describes it as "seeing and studying art in the making."

Closing. The exhibition's last day is Sunday 22 November.

Visiting

  • Venue: Tesa 41, Arsenale Militare, Fondamenta Case Nuove, Castello 2737, 30122 Venezia
  • Dates: until 22 November 2026
  • Hours: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00–17:30; closed Mondays
  • On foot: about eight minutes from the crossing at the Piraeus Lion, through the Arsenale
  • By water taxi: from the North Lagoon through Rio delle Galeazze only, calling ahead (armenianpavilion.org/visit)

Journalists can book a studio visit or an interview with Zadik Zadikian or Aram Zadikian through the press contact below.

  • Studio: Aram Zadikian, Director, Zadik Zadikian Studio, with seven artist's assistants from the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia

visit.title: Studio visits and interviews
visit.html:
Booking

Write to pressoffice@armenianpavilion.org or send a WhatsApp message to +1 323 404 1152. Please include:

  • your name and outlet;
  • the day you would like to come (Tuesday to Sunday) and a rough time;
  • who you would like to speak with: Zadik Zadikian, Aram Zadikian, or both;
  • whether you are bringing a photographer, a camera crew or sound equipment;
  • how you are arriving: on foot or by water taxi.

Visits take place during opening hours, Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00–17:30. The studio is closed on Mondays. Calls and video interviews can be arranged on other days.

What you will see

On a typical working day:

  • plaster is mixed and poured into moulds, with the pigment mixed through the material;
  • cast units are sanded and finished at the workbenches;
  • stacks are built, taken apart and built again; the units are never fixed to each other;
  • Zadik Zadikian works alongside his assistants, seven students of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia, with Aram Zadikian running the studio.

What is on the floor changes from week to week. In October the studio made an Italian flag and carried a stair of seven steps into Tesa 41. Ask us what is in progress when you book.

Interviews

  • Zadik Zadikian, artist: English
  • Aram Zadikian, Director, Zadik Zadikian Studio: English

Closing

The exhibition closes on Sunday 22 November 2026.

Getting in

Address: Tesa 41, Arsenale Militare, Fondamenta Case Nuove, Castello 2737, 30122 Venezia

On foot: start at the crossing by the Piraeus Lion and follow the route through the Arsenale to Tesa 41, about eight minutes. Map: armenianpavilion.org/visit

By water taxi: the taxi must come from the North Lagoon and enter through Rio delle Galeazze; no other entrance is allowed. Tell us when you book, and the driver must call ahead before entering the Arsenale. The driver card is on armenianpavilion.org/visit.

studio.title: Six months in Tesa 41
studio.html:
Since 9 May the Armenian Pavilion at Biennale Arte 2026 has been a working sculpture studio. Zadik Zadikian makes his work in Tesa 41, a brick hall with timber trusses in the Arsenale, in front of visitors, Tuesday to Sunday. Nothing in the room is fixed to the walls or the floor.

The basic element is a plaster unit, cast by hand and pigmented through its full depth, so the colour runs right through the material. Units are stacked, taken down and stacked again. A stack may stand for a day.

On the floor now is Who's Afraid of Red, Yellow, and Blue? Remembering Barnett Newman! (2026), a triptych in plaster, acrylic, pure pigment and EPS foam. Beside it are Big Red Bed Where Dreams Come True (2026) and a green unit standing in front of a leaning red slab. In a corner of the hall is Seven Steps to Heaven, a white stair of seven steps that leads nowhere. An Italian flag in green, white and red is being built from units.

The work has not been continuous. Visa delays kept the team away for much of the summer, and the studio returned to full production in September. Everything that reaches Tesa 41 comes on foot or by boat and is carried in by hand.

Tony Shafrazi, the pavilion's curator, describes it as "seeing and studying art in the making." The studio is open until Sunday 22 November.

serra.title: Zadikians: Richard Serra's studio, 1973–74
serra.html:
Zadik Zadikian came to New York in 1973 and began working as an assistant to Richard Serra. Serra was then taking drawing off the sheet and onto the wall: unstretched Belgian linen covered in black paintstick, stapled up and cut to fit the room. Zadikian worked on those drawings.

In 1974 Serra titled one of his first installation drawings Zadikians. It is now in the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York (Panza Collection). He titled another Shafrazi. Both were shown at Leo Castelli's gallery from 12 to 26 October 1974, in Serra's first exhibition of drawings. In 2011 Serra described Abstract Slavery (1974) as "the result of the collective effort of Zadik Zadikian, Tony Shafrazi, and myself." The title, Zadikian recalls, came from Shafrazi's description of the work.

Zadikian also recalls suggesting the idea behind the drawings to Serra: "Why don't you make your paper become your figure, and the wall become the ground?" That is his account. The record shows his name on a Serra title in a museum collection.

It was in Serra's studio that Zadikian met Tony Shafrazi, in 1973, after Serra and Shafrazi came back from Texas, where they had helped Nancy Holt complete Robert Smithson's Amarillo Ramp. Zadikian remembers Serra introducing Shafrazi as "Armenian as well." Shafrazi put it in print in 1984: "Richard Serra introduced me to Zadik Zadikian in 1973."

Serra died in March 2024. Fifty-three years after that meeting, Shafrazi is the curator of Zadikian's pavilion in Venice.

tehran.title: Gold Bricks, Tehran, 1978
tehran.html:
In the summer of 1978 Zadik Zadikian spent three months in Tehran, where Tony Shafrazi was preparing to open a gallery. At a brickworks outside the city he watched workers stack raw clay bricks to dry, with gaps left between them so the air could pass. "This is a fantastic way of stacking," he recalls thinking.

He had about a thousand bricks made by a local brick company, sanded them and covered them in gold leaf. Gold Bricks opened on 31 October 1978 at the Tony Shafrazi Gallery, Tehran. The city had been under martial law since September. It was the gallery's first exhibition and its only one: the Shah left Iran a few months later and the gallery did not reopen. After the Revolution the bricks were stolen from storage. "We lost each and every brick in the revolution," Zadikian told ARTnews in 2025.

What he kept from Tehran was the gap. His units have been stacked with space between them ever since. "I leave spaces between my blocks, my units, so that they can breathe," he says.

A year after Tehran, on 16 October 1979, Zadikian opened Shafrazi's New York gallery. Zadik Zadikian: Sculptures was the first exhibition of the Tony Shafrazi Gallery in New York, and it showed stacks of bricks he had cast by hand. The same gallery later gave Keith Haring his first major solo exhibition (1982) and, in Champions (1983), showed Zadikian alongside Jean-Michel Basquiat, Haring and Kenny Scharf.

downtown.title: Rooms in yellow and gold: New York, 1973–78
downtown.html:
Before Zadik Zadikian made units, he made rooms.

At 112 Greene Street, the artist-run space in SoHo, he painted the whole gallery yellow, fixtures and all, and opened it to the street (1973–74). He calls the piece Yellow Space. "I removed the windows off the frames… so the place would breathe," he recalls. On 9 November 1974 he made Billboard Painting at 111 Varick Street for Alanna Heiss's Institute for Art and Urban Resources.

In the mid-1970s he covered his own apartment and studio in industrial gold foil. Walls, ceilings, pipes, the radiator and the water heater all went gold. He received a CAPS grant for the gilded studio in 1975, and the gold rooms at 9 Jay Street date from 1975–76. "It was covered, unified, very democratic," he says.

Next came P.S.1, the former public school in Long Island City that opened as an art space in 1976. Zadikian gilded its entrance, and by his account it stayed gold for about five years. The gold was in place by April 1978, and P.S.1's records list him in its Special Projects of winter 1978.

The bricks of P.S.1 led him to the unit. "This is built with bricks, why don't I just start gilding bricks… That's how I got into units," he says.

None of these rooms survives. They were made for one place and later painted over or taken down, like much of the work made downtown in those years. Photographs are what remains.

accademia.title: Seven assistants from the Accademia
accademia.html:
In the 1970s Zadik Zadikian was Richard Serra's assistant. In Venice he has seven assistants of his own. All seven are students at the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia, working in the Armenian Pavilion under a convention with the Accademia.

They do the studio's daily work in public, Tuesday to Sunday. They mix and pour plaster, pigment the units and sand them. They cut EPS foam forms, print parts in resin and build in timber. Every piece then has to be carried into Tesa 41 by hand. In October the team brought Seven Steps to Heaven along the quay in sections, then skimmed, sanded and painted it white in the studio.

The team also talks about what it is making, and the studio films those conversations. Standing in front of the stair, one of the team said: "I think that the ultimate point of a sculpture like this is that, being devoid of points of reference, you fill it with yourself." Another called the work a viaggio, a trip: "There is a start, there is a finish, but the finish is not so clear."

Zadikian knows the job from the other side. In 1974 Serra titled one of his installation drawings Zadikians, after the assistant who had helped make it. Fifty years later the question of who makes the work is part of the daily life of the pavilion.

Interviews with students, in Italian or English, can be arranged before the pavilion closes on Sunday 22 November.

armenia.title: Yerevan to Venice: RETURN and the national participation
armenia.html:
Zadik Zadikian left Soviet Armenia in 1965. Sixty years later, RETURN (5 May – 1 December 2025) at the Cafesjian Center for the Arts in Yerevan showed his Foreigners series (2015–17), gilded clay figures. The Center describes it as his first exhibition in Armenia.

In October 2025 a national jury chose his project, from seven submissions, to represent the Republic of Armenia at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia. It was first announced as Ode to Lord Byron, after the poet who studied Armenian with the monks of San Lazzaro degli Armeni, the island monastery in the Venetian lagoon. By March 2026 the title was The Studio. The commissioner is Svetlana Sahakyan of the Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sport. The curators are Tony Shafrazi and Tina Chakarian.

Armenia has taken part in La Biennale as a nation since 1995. In 2015 its pavilion, Armenity, on San Lazzaro, received the Golden Lion for best national participation.

Armenia has run through Zadikian's work for decades. In the 1980s he made gilded heads and reliefs after Armenian kings, including Tigran the Great (1980). "Maybe because I was missing Armenia a great deal… or I was looking for identity," he says of those years.

In Venice the units carry no national symbols. A proposed work, Armenian Flag Stack (2026), would stack pigmented plaster units in the colours of the Armenian flag. One rendering places it in Republic Square, Yerevan.

tricolore.title: The Italian flag walks through Venice
tricolore.html:
Pavilion of the Republic of Armenia at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia

Zadik Zadikian: The Studio. The Italian flag walks through Venice

Venice, 11 November 2026

Since 5 November the Armenian Pavilion has been taking its work out into the city on foot. Sections of an Italian flag in green, white and red, made in the studio at Tesa 41, Arsenale Militare, are strapped to frames and carried on people’s backs through the campi, fondamente and rive of Venice. Set down side by side, they make the flag.

Zadik Zadikian: The Studio, the National Participation of the Republic of Armenia, has been a working sculpture studio open to the public since May. Zadik Zadikian and his team built the flag there from separate units that stand on their own feet and that two people can lift. In Venice everything is carried by hand or by boat. The walks take the flag where the city carries everything else: on people’s backs.

The walks so far. On 22 October Aram Zadikian, who runs the studio, carried a single red unit out of Tesa 41 as a test. On Thursday 5 November students of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia carried the flag, one green unit, one white and one red, to San Francesco della Vigna, Campo Santi Giovanni e Paolo and Campo Santa Maria Formosa. A passer-by called it “a travelling flag”. “It’s a journey,” Zadikian said. “We are taking a journey in Venice.” On Friday 6 November six sections went out through the Arsenale gate to the Museo Storico Navale and the Giardini.

Saturday 14 November: to Piazza San Marco. The flag leaves Tesa 41 at 11:00, walks along the Riva degli Schiavoni to Piazza San Marco and comes home another way. Anyone may walk alongside: meet at the door of Tesa 41 on the Fondamenta Case Nuove at 10:50.

Wednesday 18 November: to the Accademia. The Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia hosts Walking the Work Through Venice, a performance and meeting with the artist, promoted by Prof. Gianpaolo Mazzoni, Professor of Sculpture. Students of his sculpture course, who helped make the works in the studio, carry them on their backs from the pavilion to the Academy. They leave Tesa 41 at 10:00. From 11:00 to 12:00 the works are presented in the cloister (Aula 1 if it rains), in a meeting with professors and students, and then walk back to the pavilion. The hour in the cloister is for the Academy’s students and staff; journalists who wish to attend can write to the press office.

The walks go on until the closing day, Sunday 22 November. Each one leaves Tesa 41, sets the works down in a campo, on a fondamenta or before a church, and comes home another way. “We are turning people’s heads around,” Zadikian says. The schedule and routes are at armenianpavilion.org/walks.

In Minor Keys, the 61st International Art Exhibition conceived by Koyo Kouoh, is built around listening, slowness and work made in common. The curators of the Armenian Pavilion, Tony Shafrazi and Tina Chakarian, treat the studio itself as the exhibit: plaster is cast, pigmented, sanded and stacked in front of visitors on every open day. The walks take that public making out of the door.

Zadikian was born in Yerevan and left Soviet Armenia in 1965. In New York from 1973 he was Richard Serra’s assistant, and Serra titled the installation drawing Zadikians (1974, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum) after him. Sixty years after leaving, he represents Armenia in Venice.

Films and images

  • The Weight of the Flag (2:52), the first walk, 5 November: armenianpavilion.org/films/the-weight-of-the-flag
  • The Italian Flag (2:57), building the flag in Tesa 41: armenianpavilion.org/films/italian-flag
  • Photographs of the walks with captions and credits, and films to download up to 4K: armenianpavilion.org/press/release/tricolore

Visiting

  • Venue: Tesa 41, Arsenale Militare, Fondamenta Case Nuove, Castello 2737, 30122 Venezia
  • Dates: until 22 November 2026
  • Hours: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00–17:30; closed Mondays
  • On foot: about eight minutes from the crossing at the Piraeus Lion, through the Arsenale

Journalists can book a studio visit, a place on a walk, or an interview with Zadik Zadikian or Aram Zadikian through the press contact below.

Credits

  • Artist: Zadik Zadikian
  • Curators: Tony Shafrazi, Tina Chakarian
  • Commissioner: Svetlana Sahakyan
  • Studio: Aram Zadikian, Director, Zadik Zadikian Studio, with artist’s assistants from the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia

people.name: Zadik Zadikian
people.html: Zadik Zadikian is a sculptor. He was born in Yerevan, Soviet Armenia, and lives and works in Los Angeles. He left Armenia in 1965 and reached the United States by way of Beirut. In San Francisco he worked as an assistant to the sculptor Beniamino Bufano. In New York from 1973 he was Richard Serra's assistant, and Serra titled the installation drawing Zadikians (1974, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum) after him. He opened both of Tony Shafrazi's galleries, in Tehran (1978) and New York (1979). Recent work includes Path to Nine (2024), shown in Solid Gold at the Brooklyn Museum, and RETURN (2025) at the Cafesjian Center for the Arts, Yerevan.

people.short: Zadik Zadikian, born in Yerevan, is a Los Angeles-based sculptor who works with cast, pigmented and gilded units. He assisted Richard Serra in 1970s New York and opened both of Tony Shafrazi's galleries, in Tehran (1978) and New York (1979).

people.name: Tony Shafrazi
people.html: Tony Shafrazi (b. 1943, Abadan, Iran) is an art dealer and curator. Born to Armenian parents, he studied at the Royal College of Art in London and settled in New York at the end of the 1960s. In 1973 he helped Nancy Holt and Richard Serra complete Robert Smithson's Amarillo Ramp, and that year Serra introduced him to Zadik Zadikian. He opened the Tony Shafrazi Gallery in Tehran in 1978 and in New York in 1979, both times with Zadikian. The New York gallery gave Keith Haring his first major solo exhibition (1982) and showed the paintings Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat made together (1985). He now works as Gallery Without Walls.

people.name: Tina Chakarian
people.html: Tina Chakarian is a curator based in Boston and Yerevan. Born in Beirut, she studied visual arts at UCLA and Tufts University. She has worked to advance Armenia's presence at La Biennale di Venezia since 2015, when she was part of the advisory team for Armenity, the Armenian Pavilion on the island of San Lazzaro degli Armeni that received the Golden Lion for best national participation. Since 2018 she has been Development Director of the Armenian Pavilion, raising funds and working on its exhibitions and events. She is a curator of The Studio with Tony Shafrazi.

people.name: Aram Zadikian
people.html: Aram Zadikian is the director of Zadik Zadikian Studio and the artist's son. In Venice he runs the studio in Tesa 41: production, the team of seven assistants from the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia, deliveries into the Arsenale, and the pavilion's press and website. He works beside his father on each piece, from the first drawing through the 3D model to the full-scale form, and he made most of the renderings and photographs in the pavilion's press library. Requests for studio visits and interviews go to him.

items.html: Born in Yerevan, Soviet Armenia, where he studies sculpture.
Leaves Soviet Armenia. By his account he spends months in Istanbul and then Beirut, where he makes plaster portrait busts.
Living in the San Francisco Bay Area. Works as an assistant to the sculptor Beniamino Bufano.
By his account, a solo exhibition at the gallery La Cassapanca in Rome.
Moves to New York and becomes an assistant to Richard Serra. Meets Tony Shafrazi in Serra's studio.
Paints the whole of 112 Greene Street yellow, fixtures included. He calls the piece Yellow Space.

Serra titles two installation drawings Zadikians (Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum) and Shafrazi, shown at Leo Castelli, 12–26 October. Serra later calls Abstract Slavery (1974) "the collective effort of Zadik Zadikian, Tony Shafrazi, and myself".
Billboard Painting, 111 Varick Street, New York, 9 November, organised by Alanna Heiss's Institute for Art and Urban Resources.
CAPS grant for a gilded studio. Covers his apartment and studio in industrial gold foil (9 Jay Street, 1975–76).
Listed in P.S.1's Special Projects (15 January – 18 February). His gilded entrance at P.S.1 is in place by April.
Gold Bricks, about a thousand gilded bricks, opens on 31 October at the Tony Shafrazi Gallery, Tehran, the gallery's first and only exhibition. The bricks are later stolen from storage.
Zadik Zadikian: Sculptures (16 October – 5 November), the first exhibition of the Tony Shafrazi Gallery, New York.
Solo exhibition, Tony Shafrazi Gallery (23 March – 19 April), including Tigran the Great, gilded.
Champions, Tony Shafrazi Gallery (15 January – 19 February), with Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring and Kenny Scharf.
New California Artist VIII: Zadik Zadikian. Sculpture, Newport Harbor Art Museum, with a catalogue by Paul Schimmel.
Sculpture Myths, Tony Shafrazi Gallery (13 December 1986 – 19 January 1987).
Caravan: six gilded canvases after Armenian manuscript miniatures, shown on flatbed trucks around Los Angeles.
The Foreigners series of gilded clay figures.
Path to Nine: 999 gilded plaster ingots in eighteen stacks, in Solid Gold, Brooklyn Museum (16 November 2024 – 6 July 2025).
RETURN, Cafesjian Center for the Arts, Yerevan (5 May – 1 December), described by the Center as his first exhibition in Armenia.
Made in USA, a column of gilded plaster units, with Tony Shafrazi / Gallery Without Walls at Independent 20th Century, New York (September).
In October a national jury selects his project for the Republic of Armenia at La Biennale di Venezia.

The Studio, Pavilion of the Republic of Armenia, 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia. Tesa 41, Arsenale Militare, 9 May – 22 November. Curators Tony Shafrazi and Tina Chakarian; commissioner Svetlana Sahakyan.

films.title: Jasper Johns
films.credit: Film: Bibiana Juritz and Aram Zadikian. Edit: Bibiana Juritz. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: Twelve plaster slabs, each a different colour, slot upright into a long base engraved with the name Jasper Johns: on fitting, the handshake, and an arrangement that is never the same twice.
films.html: In Tesa 41, Zadik Zadikian and Aram Zadikian stand behind a row of white plaster bases engraved "Jasper Johns", each with a slot along its top, into which slabs of plaster cast with acrylic and pure pigment stand upright. Hands lift slabs out and set them back in another order. Zadik compares the joint to a handshake; Aram speaks of a sword in a sheath, of repetition, and of an arrangement that will not come again. English subtitles are burned in.

films.title: Seven Steps to Heaven
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: A stair of seven steps that goes nowhere, carried by hand into Tesa 41 and painted white: on cubes, journeys, the present, and a climb to heaven in a small space.
films.html: The studio team unloads the white sections of a seven-step stair and carries them through the Arsenale into Tesa 41. Zadik Zadikian measures and places them against the corner of two walls, and the team fills and paints them white. Assistants talk about cubes, journeys and the present, and about a stair that leads nowhere. English subtitles are burned in.

films.title: The Italian Flag
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: Zadik Zadikian and the studio paint and build an Italian flag from separate green, white and red units that stand on their own feet.
films.html: In Tesa 41, Zadik Zadikian and assistants spread green and red paint over large white panels, then build the flag from units that two people can lift, carry and set upright. Between the work, Zadikian talks with Aram Zadikian and with visitors about where the idea came from and about blocks of colour. English subtitles are burned in.

films.title: Carrying
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: Aram Zadikian carries a tall red unit on his back from Tesa 41 through the Arsenale and the streets of Castello, and back.
films.html: Aram Zadikian straps a tall red unit to a backpack frame in Tesa 41 and walks it out of the pavilion. He crosses the wooden bridge at the Arsenale gate, passes the stone lions and goes on through the streets of Castello, stopping to talk on the way. Zadik Zadikian walks with him. The film ends back in the studio.

films.title: Murano
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: A visit to a glass furnace on Murano, and a conversation at lunch about glass, artists and the people who make it.
films.html: Glassblowers shape a dark glass piece at the furnace while Zadik Zadikian and his guests watch. At a table outside, two men talk about glass as a material, about shopkeepers and artists, and about glass made to be collected. The film ends back in Tesa 41, where the team paints and moves flag units. English subtitles are burned in.

films.title: Before the Flag
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: Zadik and Aram Zadikian talk over a white model in Tesa 41: heights, roofs and the city.
films.html: In Tesa 41, Zadik Zadikian and Aram Zadikian stand on either side of a white foam model with a stepped, notched top. They talk about heights, about the feeling of standing on a roof in the city, and about what the shape brings to mind. Shots of the lagoon follow. English subtitles are burned in.

films.title: In Tesa 41
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: A working day in Tesa 41: fitting white units together, mixing pigment and casting, and deliveries brought in by hand.
films.html: Tall white units are fitted together on the floor of Tesa 41. Assistants pour pigment, cast and check small units at the workbench, and a parcel comes up a bridge on a hand trolley. Boats pass on a Venetian canal. Zadik Zadikian stands beside a piece and explains it. The film closes on the studio's title card.

films.title: The Maquette
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: Zadik Zadikian works out a full-size maquette in white foam at a foam-cutting plant, months before Venice.
films.html: The film opens on a 3D model on screen, pink units and gilded bricks. In a foam-cutting plant, Zadik Zadikian sets out large white blocks, adds small steps and feet, checks proportions on his phone and explains the forms to camera. Cutting machines and stacks of foam fill the background.

films.title: Leaning Red
films.credit: Film: Aram Zadikian. Courtesy Zadik Zadikian Studio
films.line: Zadik Zadikian and two helpers build a full-size cardboard mock-up of Leaning Red and stand it against a wall.
films.html: Outdoors, Zadik Zadikian measures, cuts and tapes sheets of honeycomb cardboard into a tall slab with two helpers. The mock-up is carried inside and leaned against a wall to check its height and angle, with a narrow blue unit beside it. There is no speech; the soundtrack is music only.
